title: HTTP status codes (from 200 to 418)
description:
Every web request ends with a three digit number. Byte and Compy decode them, including the teapot.

#http #webdev #programming #shorts
angle: The first digit of an HTTP status code tells you who owns the problem: nobody, you, or the server.
hook: You've seen 404. But what are all those other numbers a server sends back?

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: You've seen 404. But what are all those other numbers a server sends back?

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: Every response starts with one. We'll cover the first digit, the famous ones, and the teapot.

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: I'll guess. Two means good, four means bad.

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: Better. Two means success, four means you sent a bad request, five means the server failed.

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: So 404 means I asked for a page that isn't there.

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: Yes. And 500 means the server broke while trying. That one is rarely your fault.

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: What does the three hundred range do?

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: Redirects. The page lives somewhere else now, and your browser follows along without bothering you.

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: Okay, now the teapot. Is that real?

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: Real, and a joke. It came from an April Fools' RFC in 1998 about brewing coffee over a network.

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: Rule of the day: read the first digit before you panic.

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: Follow for more. Next: what really happens when you type a URL.

claims.text: HTTP status codes are grouped by first digit: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
418 I'm a teapot comes from the April Fools' RFC 2324 (Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol), 1998
